title: The Dharma Door of Perfect Penetration Through the Ear-Faculty
author: Zhanran
excerpt: Once one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties are all liberated.

inline.s: "Once one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties are all liberated."
At the Surangama Assembly,

after his attendant Ananda had fallen under the spell of the daughter of Matangi and had been rescued, Śākyamuni Buddha patiently and skillfully taught him again and again: the key to liberation lies in
realizing the self-nature (the tathagatagarbha)

Note: How Ananda fell under the spell of the daughter of Matangi. While Ananda was begging for food with his almsbowl, the daughter of Matangi bewitched him with a magic spell, intending to lead him into sexual pleasure. The Buddha sent Manjushri Bodhisattva to rescue Ananda with a divine mantra.
How, then, is the self-nature to be realized? Ananda and the whole assembly heard the Buddhas of the ten directions, countless as motes of dust, declare with one voice:

"You wish to know how the root of the knot that is beginningless ignorance keeps you turning through birth and death: it is none other than your six faculties, and nothing else. You also wish to know how supreme bodhi can swiftly bring you to the bliss of liberation, to tranquil wondrous permanence: that too is your six faculties, and nothing else."

(Paraphrase: You should know that the root of the knot of beginningless ignorance, which makes you turn through birth and death, is your six faculties and nothing else. You should also know that supreme bodhi, which can swiftly bring you to the bliss of liberation, to tranquil wondrous permanence, is likewise the six faculties and nothing else.) What this means is: to untie the knot of birth and death (to end segmental birth and death), you must begin with the six faculties; to realize the fruit of the bodhi path (to end transformation birth and death), you must also begin with the six faculties.
Therefore
realizing the self-nature is
a matter of beginning with the six faculties.

Note: (You wish to know) You should know. "Wish" means need, want; as in the saying, "The heart must be bold, yet the mind must be fine." (The six faculties: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.) (Beginningless ignorance: from time without beginning, the self-nature, through a single moment of unenlightenment, has lain in the darkness of the long night, not understanding the truth, and is able to give rise to every delusion and affliction; this is beginningless ignorance (ignorance coeval with birth), also called beginningless ignorance or root ignorance. The ignorance of sentient beings and the tathagatagarbha that is inherently theirs are both without beginning. The Great Vehicle Scripture on the Perfection of Truth, the Six Paramitas, says:

"A fire fanned by the wind, however fierce, can be mastered; the waves of the sea can be stilled; only the deluded mind is most difficult to tame. Why? Because beginningless ignorance deludes the mind-nature."

(Segmental birth and death: sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, owing to good and evil karma, all have lifespans of fixed limit and bodies of distinct form; hence their birth and death is called "segmental birth and death." One who ends segmental birth and death escapes the round of rebirth. Transformation birth and death: the noble ones of the three vehicles have already cut off the delusions of view and thought and ended segmental birth and death; yet in the course of cultivating the path, deluded thoughts gradually cease and realization gradually increases. This shifting between delusion and awakening differs in every period, and the passage from one period into the next is exactly like a single birth and death; its transformations are wondrous and unfathomable, beyond thought and words, and so it is called "transformation birth and death." One who ends transformation birth and death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood.)
The method is this: from
among the six faculties, choose one and penetrate deeply into it through contemplation; thus may one return to the origin and realize the self-nature. The Buddha said:

"Pull out any one faculty, and it comes free of its adhesions, turns inward and lies hidden, returning to the original truth. Then it sends forth its inherent radiance; once the nature of that radiance shines out, the other five adhesions are pulled free and liberated as well."

(Paraphrase: Choose any one faculty; do not let it adhere to deluded objects, but let it turn inward, subdue the consciousness-mind, and return to the original true mind. Then it can send forth its inherent radiance. Once the nature of that radiance shines out, it penetrates heaven and earth, illumines past and present, and is no longer stirred by the six objects. The other five faculties then no longer adhere to deluded objects or produce deluded appearances. Of themselves, along with the perfect liberation of this one faculty, they all attain perfect liberation at once.)
That is to say:
"Once one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties are all liberated."
Thereupon the Buddha asked the great Bodhisattvas and the great Arhats whose outflows were exhausted,
who were present in the assembly, to describe their methods of realization. The Buddha said

"You Bodhisattvas and Arhats who have been born in my Dharma and have attained the stage of no more learning, I now ask you: when you first brought forth the mind and awakened to the eighteen realms, which was the perfect penetration? Through what skillful means did you enter samadhi?"

Note: (Outflows exhausted) All afflictions cut off to the end. "Outflow" is another name for affliction. (No more learning) Having cut off all delusions of the three realms and realized the principle of ultimate truth, one need no longer study and cultivate the perfect wisdom. (The eighteen realms) The six faculties, the six objects, and the six consciousnesses together are called the eighteen realms.
(Samadhi) That is, sanmei.

There were twenty-five noble ones, each describing his own method of realization, giving twenty-five Dharma doors of perfect penetration in all, namely: the perfect penetrations of the six objects (form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and mental objects), the six faculties (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness), and the seven elements (earth, water, fire, wind, emptiness, seeing, and consciousness). They are:

1. The perfect penetration through the object of sound of Kaundinya and the others; 2. the perfect penetration through the object of form of Upanisad; 3. the perfect penetration through the object of fragrance of the Youth Fragrant Splendor; 4. the perfect penetration through the object of taste of the two Dharma princes, Medicine King and Medicine Superior; 5. the perfect penetration through the object of touch of Bhadrapala and the others; 6. the perfect penetration through the object of mental objects of Mahakashyapa and the others; 7. the perfect penetration through the eye-faculty of Aniruddha; 8. the perfect penetration through the nose-faculty of Chudapanthaka; 9. the perfect penetration through the tongue-faculty of Gavampati; 10. the perfect penetration through the body-faculty of Pilindavatsa; 11. the perfect penetration through the mind-faculty of Subhuti; 12. the perfect penetration through the eye-consciousness of Shariputra; 13. the perfect penetration through the ear-consciousness of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva; 14. the perfect penetration through the nose-consciousness of Sundarananda; 15. the perfect penetration through the tongue-consciousness of Purna; 16. the perfect penetration through the body-consciousness of Upali; 17. the perfect penetration through the mind-consciousness of Mahamaudgalyayana; 18. the perfect penetration through the fire element of Ucchusma; 19. the perfect penetration through the earth element of Bodhisattva Holder of the Earth; 20. the perfect penetration through the water element of the Youth Moonlight; 21. the perfect penetration through the wind element of the Dharma prince Vaidurya Light; 22. the perfect penetration through the emptiness element of Bodhisattva Akashagarbha; 23. the perfect penetration through the consciousness element of Maitreya Bodhisattva; 24. the perfect penetration through the faculty-element of Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva and the others; 25. the perfect penetration through the ear-faculty of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva.
Then the Buddha asked Manjushri Bodhisattva to choose which of these twenty-five Dharma doors was most suited to the occasion and easiest to accomplish. The Buddha said:

"I now wish to enable Ananda to awaken. Among these twenty-five practices, which one shall be his root? And for sentient beings of this world after my nirvana who enter the Bodhisattva vehicle and seek the supreme path, through what skillful door will it be easy for them to succeed?"

Because the sentient beings of the Saha world have the sharpest ear-faculty, the path by which Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva realized perfect penetration through the ear-faculty is the most suited to the occasion and the easiest to accomplish. Thus what Manjushri Bodhisattva
chose was the ear-faculty perfect penetration of Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva as foremost. Manjushri Bodhisattva
said:
"The true teaching-body of this world is pure, and it lies in sound and hearing. If one would enter samadhi,
one must truly enter through hearing
, and so escape suffering and attain liberation

You in the assembly, and Ananda too, turn round your inverted hearing-mechanism, turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature; when the nature is accomplished, it is the supreme path. Perfect penetration is truly thus.
This is the one road to nirvana’s gate of Buddhas countless as motes of dust

. The Tathagatas of the past have all accomplished this door; the Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter perfect clarity. Those who cultivate in the future should rely on this Dharma; I too have realized it by this means; it is not Avalokiteshvara alone. Truly, as the World-Honored Buddha asked me about the various skillful means, to save those of the final age who seek to transcend the world,
to accomplish the mind of nirvana,
Avalokiteshvara is foremost
The heart of the ear-faculty perfect penetration is "
returning the hearing
to hear the self-nature
." The sutra says:
Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature; when the nature is accomplished, it is the supreme path.
So the key is:
returning the hearing.
Note: (Returning the hearing to hear the self-nature)
Turn back the deluded hearing that follows sounds outward (outer hearing), and hear the self-nature within.

(When the nature is accomplished, it is the supreme path) Because the hearing is returned to the self-nature, the self-nature is transformed from the state of consciousness-nature into the state of inherent nature (returning to the origin), and thus one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood (the supreme path). (The supreme path) The path attained by the Tathagata, beyond which there is none higher; hence it is called the supreme path. The Lotus Sutra says:
"Again and again I think to myself: by what means may sentient beings enter the supreme path and swiftly accomplish the Buddha-body?"
The sutra also says:
"That Buddha taught me to enter samadhi through hearing, contemplating, and cultivating."
Note especially that here
means
"hearing and contemplating, then cultivating"
hearing the mind’s thoughts inwardly
(contemplating)
and cultivating. In the course of this inner hearing, the mind’s thoughts
(contemplation)
come to rest, and one continues to hear inwardly; this is inwardly hearing the self-nature—
returning the hearing
to the self-nature. So the point of entry for returning the hearing to the self-nature is:
hearing the mind’s thoughts inwardly

"Hearing the mind’s thoughts inwardly," put plainly, is listening to that voice in the head. When you listen with focused continuity, that chattering voice suddenly falls silent, and the stream of deluded thoughts opens into a thought-free gap. As the practice of returning the hearing deepens, this thought-free gap gradually grows, until it becomes a stable state of no-thought. Returning the hearing within no-thought is returning the hearing to the self-nature. This is prajñā perfuming ignorance; once ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya appears at once. Leaping straight into the Tathagata’s ground, one attains the dharmakaya without passing through asankhya kalpas; hence it is called the perfect and sudden Dharma door.
Note: (Sengqi) An abbreviation of "asankhya kalpa."
The advantages of this practice are: first, it is enduring and resistant to interference
, and it is a most wonderful and enjoyable practice;
second, it brings one into samadhi

third, it enables one to attain no-thought (thoughts without thought), no-form (forms without form), and no-abiding (objects without deliberation); fourth, this is the one road to nirvana’s gate of Buddhas countless as motes of dust.
This sutra says:
"Once one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties are all liberated."
It also says:
"Beings are confused as to their
inherent hearing
, and following sounds they wander on; though Ananda’s memory was strong, he could not escape wrong thought."
It also says:
"You in the assembly, and Ananda too, turn round your
inverted hearing-mechanism

, turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature; when the nature is accomplished, it is the supreme path. Perfect penetration is truly thus. This is the one road to nirvana’s gate of Buddhas countless as motes of dust."

Note: (Once one faculty returns to its source, the six faculties are all liberated) The ear-faculty no longer takes the object of sound as its condition (once one faculty returns to its source); thus the six faculties no longer take the six objects as their conditions, and faculties and objects fall away together. (Inherent hearing) Hearing the self-nature inwardly
is inherent hearing;
following sounds and hearing outwardly is deluded hearing. (Turn round your inverted hearing-mechanism, and turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature)
Turn round your inverted, deluded hearing that follows sounds outward, and turn the hearing back inward to the self-nature.
(The one road to nirvana’s gate)
The gateway into nirvana (the perfect realization of Buddhahood).

Question: "Hearing, contemplating, and cultivating" are the three wisdoms: the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of contemplating, and the wisdom of cultivating. The wisdom of hearing is the wisdom born of hearing the Buddha-Dharma;
and
the wisdom of contemplating is the wisdom born of reflecting on the Buddha’s truth;
and
the wisdom of cultivating is the wisdom born of diligently cultivating meditative concentration;
and
so
why is "hearing, contemplating, and cultivating"
explained here as
"hearing and contemplating, then cultivating"
by hearing the mind’s thoughts inwardly?

Answer: The sutra says, "That Buddha taught me to enter samadhi through hearing, contemplating, and cultivating." If "hearing, contemplating, and cultivating" here were explained as the three wisdoms—the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of contemplating, and the wisdom of cultivating—such
an
explanation would plainly not agree with the sutra passage that follows. For the passage immediately after speaks entirely of how to
hear
, and the sutra further says:
"Receiving from that Tathagata the illusory
hearing and cultivation of hearing
, the vajra samadhi."
Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva said that his method of practice is
hearing
"By my
hearing
and contemplating, I escaped the six objects." "The Buddha asked about perfect penetration: I perfected the samadhi of illuminating reflection through the
ear-door
; the conditioned mind became free, and by entering the stream I attained samadhi and accomplished bodhi. This was foremost."
When Manjushri Bodhisattva chose the perfect penetration, he too spoke of
hearing
"I now declare to the World-Honored One: the Buddha appears in the Saha world; the true teaching-body of this world is pure, and it lies in sound and
hearing
. If one would enter samadhi, one must truly enter through
hearing
, and so escape suffering and attain liberation
Beings are confused as to their inherent
hearing
, and following sounds they wander on; though Ananda’s memory was strong, he could not escape wrong thought
You in the assembly, and Ananda too, turn round your inverted
hearing
-mechanism, turn the
hearing back to hear
the self-nature; when the nature is accomplished, it is the supreme path
All
these sutra passages speak only of
hearing
and this "hearing" is returning the hearing, hearing inwardly, not hearing by following sounds outward
, with no mention at all of contemplating and cultivating among the three wisdoms. What is more, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva clearly says that his method of practice is
hearing and contemplating
(hearing the mind’s thoughts inwardly):
"By my
hearing and contemplating
, I escaped the six objects."
How, then, is one to hear? The answer is:
return the hearing to the self-nature.
This is the
key
to correctly understanding the chapter on the ear-faculty perfect penetration. The nature is the essence, the mind is its function;
yet
the self-nature has no form,
and so
one uses hearing
to
reach the essence, and by hearing the mind’s thoughts inwardly one
enters
into
the self-nature
. That is to say

hearing and contemplating, then cultivating—hearing the thoughts within the mind; when the mind’s thoughts come to rest (entering the stream, the object vanishes), what is heard is the self-nature itself—"returning the hearing to hear the self-nature."
In the Surangama Sutra, Manjushri Bodhisattva praises Avalokiteshvara’s ear-door perfect penetration, saying:
Turn the hearing back to hear the self-nature

; when the nature is accomplished, it is the supreme path. Perfect penetration is truly thus. This is the one road to nirvana’s gate of Buddhas countless as motes of dust. The Tathagatas of the past have all accomplished this door; the Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter perfect clarity. Those who cultivate in the future should rely on this Dharma; I too have realized it by this means; it is not Avalokiteshvara alone."
And he singles it out as foremost among all the Dharma doors of perfect penetration:

"Truly, as the World-Honored Buddha asked me about the various skillful means, to save those of the final age who seek to transcend the world, to accomplish the mind of nirvana, Avalokiteshvara is foremost."

Note: (The Tathagatas of the past have all accomplished this door; the Bodhisattvas of the present now each enter perfect clarity) The Buddhas of the past have already accomplished the path by this Dharma door of ear-faculty perfect penetration; the Bodhisattvas of the present likewise each enter perfect clarity by this Dharma door.
The
essential point
of this practice is
to connect with the self-nature, and never depart from it, by returning the hearing to the self-nature.
Huineng said:
"The disciple’s own mind constantly gives rise to wisdom; never departing from the self-nature, this is the field of merit."
(The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch) The state of returning the hearing to the self-nature goes from coarse to subtle, growing deeper as one proceeds.
The Xiu Xin Jue (Essentials of Mind Cultivation) says:

"Moreover, the ways of entering the principle are many, but I will point you to one gate and let you return to the source. Do you still hear the cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies? He answered: I hear them. He said: Turn back and hear your hearing-nature; are there still many sounds? He answered: At this point, all sounds and all discriminations are utterly unobtainable. He said: How wondrous! How wondrous! This is the gate by which Avalokiteshvara entered the principle. I ask you further: when you say that at this point all sounds and all discriminations are utterly unobtainable, since they are unobtainable, at that time
(at that moment)
is it then emptiness? He answered: It was never empty; it is luminous and unobscured. He said: What is
(what is the nature of)

the substance of this non-emptiness? He answered: It has no form or mark either; words cannot reach it. He said: This is the lifespan of all Buddhas and all patriarchs; doubt it no more. ... The nature knows of itself: this is your empty, still, luminous knowing, the pure essence of mind; and this pure, empty, still mind is the supremely pure and luminous mind of the Buddhas of the three times, and it is also the original enlightened nature of sentient beings. One who awakens to it and guards it sits in suchness, unmoving and liberated; one who is deluded about it and turns away from it goes to the six destinations and wanders for long kalpas."

s.s: A Detailed Explanation of the Xiu Xin Jue

inline.s: The relevant sutra passages on the ear-faculty perfect penetration from the Surangama Sutra are now excerpted and annotated as follows:

At that time, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, I recall that countless kalpas ago, as many as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteshvara. I brought forth the mind of bodhi before that Buddha. That Buddha taught me to enter samadhi through hearing, contemplating, and cultivating. At first, in the hearing, I entered the stream and the object vanished. When what had entered was stilled, the two marks of movement and stillness no longer arose. Thus gradually increasing, hearing and what is heard came to an end. When hearing was exhausted and I did not dwell there, awareness and what is aware became empty. When emptiness and awareness were perfectly complete, emptiness and what is emptied were extinguished. When arising and ceasing were both extinguished, tranquil extinction appeared before me. Suddenly I transcended the world and what is beyond the world, and the ten directions became perfectly clear.
The
key
point of the work in the ear-faculty perfect penetration is to
return the hearing to the self-nature with focus, continuity, and endurance. First, one must understand
the three stages: "entering the stream, the object vanishes," "the two marks of movement and stillness no longer arise," and "hearing and what is heard come to an end."

At that time, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, I recall that countless kalpas ago, as many as the sands of the Ganges, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteshvara. I brought forth the mind of bodhi before that Buddha. That Buddha taught me to enter samadhi through hearing, contemplating, and cultivating.
At
that time, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva rose from his seat, bowed at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha: World-Honored One, I recall that
in
the past,
countless kalpas ago, as many as the sands of the Ganges
At that time
there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Avalokiteshvara. Before that Buddha
I brought forth the mind of bodhi. That Buddha taught me to cultivate through hearing and contemplating
the mind’s thoughts
and
thus enter samadhi.
At first, in the hearing, I entered the stream and the object vanished

In the initial stage of hearing and contemplating, then cultivating (at first, in the hearing): when the practice reaches a certain depth, as one hears inwardly (returns the hearing), the thoughts that are heard come to rest and vanish.

Hearing sounds outwardly is "flowing out"; hearing the mind’s thoughts and the self-nature inwardly (returning the hearing) is "entering the stream." The habitual tendency from beginningless kalpas is to flow out, hearing by following sounds; now one does the opposite (
"turn round your inverted hearing-mechanism"
), and single-mindedly hears inwardly—entering the stream—so as to return to the origin.

"Object" stands in contrast to "subject" and refers to what is heard. Here the "object" is the thoughts that are heard. When the work of returning the hearing (entering the stream) is slightly deepened, one need only
hear

single-mindedly, and deluded thoughts cease of themselves: this is "entering the stream, the object vanishes." After "the object vanishes," what is heard is the self-nature itself—"returning the hearing to hear the self-nature"; one senses the presence of the self-nature and becomes one with it.
Question: When returning the hearing to the self-nature, what should be done if deluded thoughts arise?
Answer: If deluded thoughts arise, it means the returning of the hearing has slackened. Rouse your spirits at once, and hear inwardly with focus and continuity,
returning the hearing upon the deluded thoughts
; the deluded thoughts will cease of themselves.
Question: How can one reach "entering the stream, the object vanishes"?

Answer: The method is this: hear the mind’s thoughts inwardly. When you hear inwardly with focus, deluded thoughts come to rest. But as soon as you relax, or your attention wanders, or you forget the inner hearing, deluded thoughts rise again, and you may even be carried away by a flight of fancy. The moment you notice, you must at once give a sharp wake-up, draw your attention back, and hear inwardly with focus once more; then the deluded thoughts come to rest again. Practicing in this way over and over, the attention of inner hearing is lost and recovered, lost and recovered, and the deluded thoughts rise and cease, rise and cease. As the practice of returning the hearing deepens, the periods of focused, continuous inner hearing grow longer and longer, and the state of no-thought is sustained longer and longer. Deluded thoughts always arise in the gaps where the inner hearing is not continuous; so the core of returning the hearing at this stage is to make the inner hearing of the mind’s thoughts focused, continuous, and enduring. It must be practiced while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. Practice it long, until the practice becomes a single piece: that is the state of "entering the stream, the object vanishes."

This practice is most wonderful: whenever there is noise in the head (deluded thoughts), it is a most irritating thing that ordinary people can do nothing about; yet if you only hear inwardly with focus, listening to what it is saying, the noise vanishes at once.
This is truly a remarkable discovery:
the button that stops deluded thoughts—returning the hearing!
Press it, and the deluded thoughts come to rest.
Once the practice of returning the hearing has taken hold, there will come an experience
of effortless no-thought.
Note: (Once your practice of returning the hearing has taken hold)

When one can hear inwardly without interruption for a short span of time, that is, when the inner hearing is continuous, the practice of returning the hearing is said to have taken hold. Before this, the returning of the hearing is a moment of hearing and a moment of interruption (no hearing), the two alternating (so that one feels one is returning the hearing and thinking deluded thoughts at the same time), and one may even be dragged away by deluded thoughts and forget the returning of the hearing altogether. Deluded thoughts arise precisely where the returning of the hearing is interrupted, and blaze up when it is forgotten.
When what had entered was stilled, the two marks of movement and stillness no longer arose.

The thoughts of the returning hearing (what had entered) have already come to rest (been stilled), and the two marks of the arising of a thought (the mark of movement) and the ceasing of a thought (the mark of stillness) do not arise at all. At this point the state of "the object vanishes" has become quite stable, and the practice has become a single piece.

Note: (The two marks of movement and stillness) The two marks that things possess. The mark of movement: an event occurs and proceeds. The mark of stillness: an event ends and comes to rest. Here the "event" is a thought. The mark of movement is the arising of a thought; the mark of stillness is the ceasing of a thought.
(Utterly) Wholly, entirely. For example, "utterly without hearing" means not hearing at all.
Thus gradually increasing, hearing and what is heard came to an end.
The practice of
returning the hearing to the self-nature grows deeper and deeper, until the hearer and what is heard are both extinguished—subject and object both perish
and one realizes "hearing and what is heard come to an end."
Note: (Hearing and what is heard come to an end) The
hearing
and the
heard
are both extinguished, and faculty and object fall away together.
Chan Master Baizhang, ascending the hall, said:

"The spiritual light shines alone, utterly free of faculty and object. The essence is revealed in true permanence, bound by no words. The mind-nature is undefiled, perfect from the first. Simply be free of deluded conditions, and you are the Buddha of suchness."
(The Five Lamps Meeting the Source)
Note: (Utterly free of faculty and object)
The six faculties and the six objects fall away completely

. (Deluded conditions) To condition oneself on things deludedly; here "to condition" is a verb. (Simply be free of deluded conditions, and you are the Buddha of suchness) If one is simply free of deluded conditioning, one is the dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
"The Dharma Buddha
(the dharmakaya Buddha)
is free of conditioning."
The Diamond Sutra says:
"Free of all marks, one is named a Buddha."
(The Buddha of suchness) The Buddha who is awakened to the principle of suchness, that is, the dharmakaya Buddha. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
"What is the manifested Buddha? What is the reward-born Buddha? What is the Buddha of suchness?"
The fourth and fifth stages that follow strip away, layer by layer.
When hearing was exhausted and I did not dwell there, awareness and what is aware became empty.

Though hearing and what is heard are exhausted, one does not linger in the state of "exhausted hearing"; one rouses the awareness and illumination and presses on. Then the thought of awareness and the objects of that awareness no longer exist
and one realizes "awareness and what is aware are empty."
Note: (Exhausted hearing) The hearer
and the heard
are both extinguished
. (Awareness and what is aware are empty) The aware and the object of awareness are both extinguished.
When emptiness and awareness were perfectly complete, emptiness and what is emptied were extinguished.
Though awareness
and
its object
are both
emptied, one must not
linger in the state of "emptying awareness." Press on:
let
"the emptying of awareness"
itself, this emptiness,
also
be emptied,
so as to enter the state of perfect completeness, and realize
"emptiness and what is emptied are extinguished."
Note: (Emptiness and what is emptied are extinguished) The emptying and the emptied
are both extinguished.
When arising and ceasing were both extinguished, tranquil extinction appeared before me.
Thereupon
the arising and ceasing of the mind’s thoughts (including the subtle thoughts) come wholly to rest
, and one realizes and enters the state of tranquil extinction—nirvana—of permanence, bliss, true self, and purity.

Note: (Tranquil extinction) Tranquil extinction is nirvana. To be without affliction is called "tranquil"; to be without birth and death is called "extinction." The state in which there is neither affliction nor birth and death is nirvana. The Lankavatara Sutra says:
"What I teach is that when the deluded consciousness ceases, it is named nirvana."
When arising and ceasing are both extinguished

, tranquil extinction appeared before me) When the arising and ceasing of the mind’s thoughts (including the subtle thoughts) come wholly to rest, the great dream is awakened, and one realizes and enters the state of tranquil extinction—nirvana—of permanence, bliss, true self, and purity.

(Subtle thoughts) There are three kinds of mind-thoughts: coarse thoughts, fine thoughts, and subtle thoughts. For a Buddha-reciter, for example, deluded thoughts are coarse thoughts, and the thought of the recitation is a fine thought. When coarse and fine thoughts both cease, this is commonly called no-thought; this is what "no-thought" generally means. Further, if the subtle thoughts also come to rest, this is ultimate no-thought. So the meaning of the word "no-thought" must be determined from its context. The "no-thought" of "the original mind is no-thought" means ultimate no-thought. (Subtle thoughts) The subtle arising and ceasing, the flowing and changing, of the consciousness-mind; this is the mark of the alaya-consciousness. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana says:
"When the Bodhisattva’s ground is exhausted
(the ten grounds fully cultivated)
, and skillful means are fulfilled, with a single thought corresponding, the enlightened mind first arises, and that mind has no initial mark;
because it is far removed from subtle thoughts,
one sees the mind-nature
, and the mind abides forever;
this is called ultimate enlightenment
Great Master Guifeng said:
"If the subtle flow
(the subtle thoughts)

is wholly stilled, and only the great perfect-enlightenment wisdom shines alone, then one manifests hundreds of billions of bodies according to capacity to deliver sentient beings who have the conditions, and this is called a Buddha."

[Suddenly I transcended the world and the world-transcending, and the ten directions were round and bright.]
Suddenly I transcended the world and the world-transcending, and the ten directions were perfectly bright and complete.
[Ten directions, round and bright]
I and

the worlds of the ten directions merge without obstruction. The whole earth is the radiance of my own nature, and all of space is the substance and form of my own nature. All the dharmas of the ten directions are none other than the radiance of my own nature, all-pervading and perfectly complete.

[I attained two supreme excellences: first, above, I united with the wondrous enlightened true mind of all the Buddhas of the ten directions and shared the same compassionate power as all the Tathagatas; second, below, I united with all living beings of the six realms and shared the same compassionate yearning of all sentient beings.]

I attained two supreme excellences: First, above, I united with the originally wondrous, enlightened true mind realized by all the Buddhas of the ten directions, possessing the same compassionate power as all the Buddhas. Second, below, I united with all living beings of the six realms (mind joined with theirs, responsive to every appeal), sharing the same compassionate yearning as all sentient beings (feeling within myself their suffering and their longing to escape suffering and attain bliss).
Possessing both
the sacred power to draw forth the suffering of all living beings and to give bliss to all living beings,
and

feeling within herself the suffering of all living beings and their longing to escape pain and attain joy, this is our great compassionate, great merciful Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva who rescues us from suffering.

[Two supreme excellences: above, one with all the Buddhas; below, one with all beings.] [Compassionate power: the power to draw forth the suffering of all beings and to give bliss to all beings.] [Compassionate yearning: ‘bei’ is sorrow, ‘yang’ is longing; beings, in the torment of suffering, grieve over their pain and long to attain bliss.] [Responsive to every appeal: when beings, with a deep mind, pray with pure karmic causes for Avalokiteshvara’s compassionate deliverance, their longing heart immediately resonates with and perfectly accords with Avalokiteshvara’s unconditioned great compassion; the channel of communication receiving Avalokiteshvara’s empowerment is thereby unimpeded. Hence the unobstructed wondrous function and effortless wondrous power realized by Avalokiteshvara — transcending every obstruction in the world — can bless them, arouse the unobstructed wondrous function originally inherent in their mind-nature, and so manifest as the inconceivable resonance that surpasses the obstacles of worldly matter, time, and space.]
